Q: How to start a Uvicorn + FastAPI in background when testing with PyTest A:

Cross-posting from the (kinda) related Uvicorn cannot be shutdown programmatically GitHub discussion, I scrapped together something that can work with/without Python.

from fastapi import FastAPI
import asyncio
import uvicorn
import aiohttp
from datetime import datetime
import random
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

async def fetch(session:aiohttp.ClientSession, url):
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        data = await response.text()
        return data
    
async def test(n_reqs:int=1):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        tasks = [fetch(session, 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/') for _ in range(n_reqs)]

        print('Fetching results...')
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

        for i, result in enumerate(results):
            print(f'Result {i}: {result}')

app = FastAPI()

@app.get('/')
async def root():
    await asyncio.sleep(random.randint(1, 5))
    return f'Current time: {datetime.now()}'

@asynccontextmanager
async def running_server(server:uvicorn.Server):
    print('Starting server...')
    asyncio.create_task(server.serve())

    try:
        while not server.started:
            # give server some time to start up
            await asyncio.sleep(1e-3)
        yield # server started - do some other stuff
    finally:
        print('Shutting down server...')
        server.should_exit = True
        await server.shutdown()

async def main():
    n_reqs = 7

    config = uvicorn.Config(app, loop=asyncio.get_running_loop())
    server = uvicorn.Server(config)

    async with running_server(server):
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(test(n_reqs=n_reqs))

    print('All done!')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    asyncio.run(main())

Mainly inspired by this great SO answer. uvicorn can run from an existing asyncio environment so if we start the event loop ourselves then we can control when the server starts and shuts down. So we can make our own async context manager that starts the server (in a task), yields control back to event loop so other code can run, then tells the server to shut itself down when there's nothing more to do in context.

You can also get this to work w/ pytest, so long as you install pytest-asyncio. Here's what it looks like:

import asyncio
import pytest
import pytest_asyncio
import aiohttp
import random
from fastapi import FastAPI
import uvicorn
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from typing import Literal
from fastapi.responses import PlainTextResponse

app = FastAPI()

@app.get('/', response_class=PlainTextResponse)
async def root():
    await asyncio.sleep(random.randint(1, 4))
    return 'Hello world!'

@app.get('/foo')
async def foo():
    await asyncio.sleep(random.randint(1, 4))
    return {'a':1}

async def fetch(session:aiohttp.ClientSession, url:str, content_type:Literal['text', 'json']='text'):
    print(f'Fetching {content_type} response...')
    async with session.get(url) as response:
        res = None
        match content_type:
            case 'text':
                res = await response.text()
            case 'json':
                res = await response.json()
            case _:
                raise ValueError(f'Unknown content type {content_type}')
        return res
    print(f'{content_type} response fetched!')

@asynccontextmanager
async def running_server(server:uvicorn.Server):
    print('Starting server...')
    asyncio.create_task(server.serve())

    try:
        while not server.started:
            # give server some time to start up
            await asyncio.sleep(1e-3)
        print('Server started!')
        yield # server started - give up control so other code can do stuff
    finally:
        print('Shutting down server...')
        server.should_exit = True
        await server.shutdown()
        print('Server shut down!')

@pytest.fixture(scope='class') # see https://docs.pytest.org/en/7.1.x/how-to/fixtures.html#fixture-scopes (VERY IMPORTANT!)
def server_cfg():
    return uvicorn.Config(app)

@pytest_asyncio.fixture(scope='class')
async def server_ctx(request:pytest.FixtureRequest, server_cfg:uvicorn.Config):
    request.cls.loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    request.cls.server_cfg = server_cfg

    server = uvicorn.Server(server_cfg)
    async with running_server(server):
        yield

@pytest.mark.asyncio(loop_scope='class')
class TestGracefulAsyncServer():
    loop: asyncio.AbstractEventLoop
    server_cfg: uvicorn.Config

    @pytest.mark.parametrize('n_reqs', [1, 3])
    async def test_root_endpoint(self, server_ctx, n_reqs:int):
        assert TestGracefulAsyncServer.loop is asyncio.get_running_loop()
        
        server_cfg = TestGracefulAsyncServer.server_cfg

        async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
            tasks = [
                fetch(
                    session, 
                    f'{"https" if server_cfg.ssl else "http"}://{server_cfg.host}:{server_cfg.port}{app.url_path_for("root")}',
                    content_type='text',
                    ) for _ in range(n_reqs)
                ]
            results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
            
            assert len(results) == n_reqs

            for res in results:
                assert res == 'Hello world!'

    @pytest.mark.parametrize('n_reqs', [1, 3])
    async def test_foo_endpoint(self, server_ctx, n_reqs:int):
        assert TestGracefulAsyncServer.loop is asyncio.get_running_loop()
        server_cfg = TestGracefulAsyncServer.server_cfg

        async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
            tasks = [
                fetch(
                    session, 
                    f'{"https" if server_cfg.ssl else "http"}://{server_cfg.host}:{server_cfg.port}{app.url_path_for("foo")}',
                    content_type='json',
                    ) for _ in range(n_reqs)
                ]
            results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
            
            assert len(results) == n_reqs

            for res in results:
                assert res == {'a':1}

The core strategy (external event loop + home-baked async context manager) is the same, hardest part is wiring together w/ pytest.

  1. pytest collects tests.
  2. First test in the test class needs server_ctx, which enters the async context manager. Again, this is where we do graceful start up and shut down.
  3. pytest-asyncio creates/activates the class-scoped event loop because we've requested it in the server_ctx fixture from request's cls attribute when we call the very first test ("Fixtures are created when first requested by a test...")
  4. server_ctx function runs. The event loop is started and mapped to the test class. Because this fixture is class-scoped, it is called once and cached by pytest then reused for subsequent tests in that class that request it. This is means the server is only started/stopped once during all testing.
  5. After class tests finish, fixture teardown stops server, async context is left, and there's nothing more to do.

Haven't tested the approach a ton so there may be pitfalls but it does run and appear to do things "gracefully" and asynchronously.

Q: Python pyc cache is not invalidated when source code is modified quickly A:

If you really wanted to modify the Python file, one solution would be to delete the pycache folder right after modifying b.py.

The easier and cleaner way to do the same thing would be to pass an argument to the file.

a.py

import sys

print(int(sys.argv[1])) # We use 1 as the index because sys.argv[0] is 'a.py'

c.sh:

for i in {1..20}; do
    sleep 0.3
    python3 a.py i
done

Alternatively, if you had to import b.py for some reason, you could store i in a file and load it in b.py.

a.py (Same):

import b
print(b.i)

b.py:

with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    i = int(f.read())

c.sh:

for i in {1..20}; do
    echo i > data.txt
    sleep 0.3
    python3 a.py
rm data.txt # Optional, if you want to clean up the file
done

Q: AWS-SSM vs SSH (security) A:

If I may clarify a couple of things. Smackin SSM on everything without thinking is what this post is about. Just like most things in life, each thing has its pros and cons.

Let's take this following scenario as an example:

let's say an internal dev team building the frontend for an app is your customer, and you are providing the backend infrastructure for them to overlay their app

Usually this would require a dev and prod environment at least! In the dev environment rapid implementation, feedback, and loops are greatly beneficial. So throwing a wrench into the dev environment may hinder this fast cycle of iterations (to say the least) - especially if the new workflow introduced doesn't match the customer's. Not only are we hindering the developers with a new workflow and custom scripts but also possibly introducing the above mentioned security issues - especially in environments where rapid development is encouraged. This being said, security should still be set in place, from a practical point of view.

Now if we take the flip side, a Production environment, likely visible to public and and the developers never touch these, updates are pushed automatically and patched automatically leaving barely any need for the frontend developers to reach the production nodes. Sure, why not stick SSM here (if some form of node access is needed).

As a side note - AWS has an option to tie ssh keys to iam roles! I haven't looked into this, but this sounds super interesting.

Q: How to fix ValueError: Found array with 0 sample(s) A:

When you do:

X = np.array(X).reshape((1,-1))
Y = np.array(Y).reshape((1,-1))

You are transforming your lists (of length N) into a 1xN array (i.e. one row, N columns). But then, when you split your dataset, you do:

X_train = X[:-250]

Which tries to select all the rows until row N-250. But since there is only one row, it puts a 0xN array into X_train. The LinearRegressionModel doesn't like that.

What you want to do is to get Nx1 arrays. With reshape, the -1 corresponds to "try to fill this dimension with whatever fits given the other constraints". So if you want N rows and 1 column, you need:

X = np.array(X).reshape((-1, 1))
Y = np.array(Y).reshape((-1, 1))

Alternatively, if you want to be more explicit about what you're doing (which is adding a new axis to the array), you can do:

X = np.array(X)[:, np.newaxis]
Y = np.array(Y)[:, np.newaxis]

Finally, your last line:

print( str(round(regressIt.predict(Y))) )

Will not work. The result of predict is a numpy array, and to round a numpy array you should use the np.round method. Also there is no need to cast to str, as that will be done automatically by print. So this would give:

print(np.round(regressIt.predict(Y)))

Q: Export to PDF and Prompt User for Folder Path and File Name to Save A:

The code below will prompt the user to select a location and filename to save the pdf as.

Dim file_name As Variant
file_name = Application.GetSaveAsFilename(FileFilter:="Adobe PDF File_ (*.pdf), *.pdf")

If file_name <> False Then
  ActiveWorkbook.SaveAs Filename:=file_name
  MsgBox "File Saved!"
End If
